newsitem.title: USA: American Lung Assoc to fight air standards delay.
newsitem.headline: American Lung Assoc to fight air standards delay.

text.p: The American Lung Association said Monday it would fight the Environmental Protection Agency's request to a federal court to give it more time to set air quality standards.

The Lung Association, which originally sued the EPA to push it to review its air standards, said it would ask the court to hold the EPA to a court-ordered June deadline to issue a new rule against soot and smog air pollution.
The association said it endorsed a 30-day extension of the public comment period, now set to end Feb. 18, as long as the final rule were issued in June.

"It is time for the Environmental Protection Agency to carry out its legal responsibility without further delay to make sure our air is really safe to breathe," Fran Du Melle, the Lung Association's managing director, said in a statement.

While she said the public should have ample time to comment on the standards, Du Melle said: "For months the polluters have been lobbying governors, the EPA, the White House and the Congress. They want a delay so they can continue lobbying behind closed doors to destroy these standards."

Bowing to a request from the National Governors Association, the EPA over the weekend said it would ask a federal court in Arizona to let the agency extend the public comment period by 60 days, and push back the deadline for issuing final standards by that amount of time as well.
The Lung Association's original lawsuit -- which produced the June court-ordered deadline for a final air standard rule -- was filed in Arizona.
EPA Administrator Carol Browner, in a letter to the governors, said said she recognised "additional time is needed to responsibly assess and comment on our proposal."

A comment from the National Association of Manufacturers, which is spearheading efforts by industry groups to block tougher standards, was not immediately available on whether industry groups would also get involved in the court case.
Industry groups contend the proposed standards would require pollution controls that would cost billions of dollars and stifle economic growth.

An EPA official said the agency's request for an extension will be filed early this week. He said the agency expected an answer from the court before the February 18 expiration of the current public comment period.
